contexts: emergency department, about 72,000 adult attendances a year
about 4,100 adults with suspected sepsis a year
reading: The triage decision turns on two errors: a normal lactate in a patient who has sepsis (false reassurance, c2) and a raised lactate in a patient who does not (false alarm, which fills the resuscitation area; c5 hints at this). Accuracy depends on the threshold and on who is tested (c1), and capillary values drift from venous ones at high levels. The reviews that should settle this share their primary studies (c3) and mostly deserve low confidence (c4), so their disagreement is largely about definitions, not new evidence. A regional statement already forbids lowering priority on a normal value.

nodes.label: False reassurance
nodes.detail: About 9 percent of patients with lactate below 2 mmol/L had sepsis with organ dysfunction (c2).

nodes.label: False alarm
nodes.detail: Raised lactate without sepsis; cost to other patients.

nodes.label: Regional consensus statement
nodes.detail: Lactate for suspected infection plus a physiological criterion.

summary: Map of the two triage errors, the evidence that quantifies them and the overlap and confidence problems behind the disagreement.
